pedagogy.summary: By Y4, children move from naming shapes by look (van Hiele level 1) to reasoning about defining properties (level 2), and start the class-inclusion idea (level 3): a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it has every property a rectangle needs plus the extra property of four equal sides. The obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — a child sorts each shape into exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle they picture. Teaching works by shifting the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?', so category membership is decided by properties, not appearance.
bestPractices: Define categories by an explicit checklist of properties (rectangle = 4 right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and let children TEST a shape against the checklist rather than judge by eye
Use nested/overlapping Venn or set diagrams so a shape can visibly sit in two categories at once — this attacks the partition assumption that each shape belongs to exactly one box
Deliberately include non-prototypical examples: a square, a rectangle tilted 45°, a very-nearly-square rectangle, so 'rectangle' is not welded to the long-oblong prototype
Contrast examples with non-examples: ask children to draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, forcing them to reason about which properties are absent
Insist on justification in the child's own words ('it is a rectangle because...') — knowing the shared properties is the point, not the yes/no answer
keyRepresentations: Property checklist / definition card for each category (right-angle marks, equal-side tick marks, parallel arrows)
Nested Venn diagram: quadrilaterals ⊃ rectangles ⊃ squares, with rhombuses overlapping so square sits in the intersection
A 'stretchy' square that can be pulled into an oblong rectangle or squashed to a rhombus, showing square as the special case where both hold
Set-square and ruler to physically verify right angles and equal sides
commonMisconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)

learn.summary: Help Year 4 children (age 8–9) move from naming quadrilaterals by appearance to deciding category membership by property tests, and begin class-inclusion reasoning: a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it passes every rectangle test (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus has the extra property of four equal sides. The core obstacle is partition/prototype thinking — a child files each shape in exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't match the 'long oblong' they picture. Teaching shifts the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?'

activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
feedback: When a learner says a square is 'too square' to be a rectangle, walk the rectangle checklist together item by item; if it passes every test, the square belongs in the 'rectangle' ring without leaving 'square'.

If a learner thinks a rectangle must have two long and two short sides, show a run of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square, confirming each passes the same tests — length is not a defining property.

If a learner accepts the shared properties yet still won't let one shape be in two categories, offer everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog AND an animal at once) and more nested-set practice rather than drilling the yes/no fact.
Reinforce justification: the point is naming the shared properties ('four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel'), not the bare yes/no answer.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable surface lets children test a shape against a visible checklist and watch labels attach or drop as properties change — making 'membership by property, not appearance' concrete. A stretch tool that keeps the 'rectangle' label while dropping the 'square' badge, and nested rings that show one shape in two boxes at once, directly address partition and oblong-prototype thinking. Optional interaction examples (draggable handles, a checklist that ticks green as each test passes, snapping to the deepest qualifying region) make the mechanism tangible but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
Y4 pupils should compare and classify geometric shapes, including quadrilaterals, based on their properties and sizes
learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.

activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square
feedback: A correct answer is 'yes — a square is a rectangle: it has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, plus its four sides happen to be equal, so it is a special rectangle.'
If a learner judges by appearance ('it's too square-looking') and cannot state the defining properties, build the checklist together and test item by item.
For 'a square turned 45° is a diamond', confirm turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so it is still a square and still a rectangle.

When asked to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle, the learner should discover this is impossible: every square passes all the rectangle tests, so no such shape exists — whereas a rectangle that is not a square CAN be drawn. Noticing this one-way asymmetry is the sign of real property-based understanding.
Treat 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' as a maturing class-inclusion stage, not a false fact; give more nested-set experience rather than correction drills.
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain routine with a physical square, set-square and ruler makes the diagnostic reasoning visible and lets children verify right angles and equal sides themselves. Asking for the reason, not just the answer, discriminates property-based reasoning from a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'both have four sides'.

'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
learnerActions: Before testing, predict whether a square 'counts as' a rectangle and say WHY.
Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?
If the result differs from your prediction, explain what changed your mind.

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before testing exposes prototype thinking; reconciling a 'no, too square' prediction with the square passing every rectangle test is where the concept takes hold. The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.

activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
feedback: Accept a non-example only when the learner shows a defining property is missing for each category it must be excluded from. Some missing properties exclude only some categories: 'no right angles → not a rectangle or square' still leaves rhombus open, so also check 'the four sides are not all equal → not a rhombus or square'. One missing property can exclude all three: rectangles, rhombuses and squares all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so a shape without two pairs of parallel sides (e.g. a kite or trapezium) is none of them.
Accept the inclusion claim only when the learner cites the defining properties the square passes, not just that 'it looks like one' or 'both have four sides'.
If a learner cannot produce a non-prototypical rectangle, offer tilted and nearly-square examples and have them verify each against the checklist.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples with non-examples forces attention to defining versus non-defining attributes, and justification in the child's own words is the learning target. An in-role classifier who presses 'but it doesn't look like a rectangle — why does it still count?' surfaces and names the reasoning; dialogue here supports the property inspection rather than replacing it.

Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
learnerActions: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about which properties are ABSENT (for non-examples) and which are PRESENT (for inclusion) consolidates definition-based classification and loosens the oblong prototype.

constraints: Target concept is property-based classification and class inclusion, not shape naming; always require justification by defining properties, not a bare yes/no.

A scored sort/multiple-choice can assess whether a child accepts the inclusion (e.g. 'Is a square a rectangle?' with distractor 'No, they are different shapes') but does not by itself let the child feel a square pass the tests; use it to check, not to build, the insight.

A static tap-to-reveal Venn or hierarchy is a useful summary/reference showing where a square sits, but because nothing recomputes the child cannot TEST a shape's membership; best used after hands-on testing rather than as the primary route.

Distinguish an ideal zero-thickness plane figure from physical card/cutouts, which have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat cutouts as approximations of the represented flat shape and ask about the mathematical shape represented, not whether the physical card can be picked up. Quadrilateral classification is a planar, 2D property idea, so a third spatial dimension is not needed here (a limit of relevance, not evidence that any one medium is superior).
Treat the one-box (class-inclusion) stage as developmental: give more nested-set and everyday-inclusion experience rather than drilling the fact.
Set-square/ruler verification and recolouring/ticking checklists are optional supports to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum Year 4 Geometry) is marked verified:false in the row; treat that claim with corresponding caution.

The row frames the topic as Year 4 (age 8–9) while citing Common Core 5.G.3/5.G.4 (Grade 5) for hierarchy/subcategory attributes; this grade-band mismatch is a migration ambiguity, though the inclusion content is consistent with the stated evidence targets.

The original 'poor fit / 3D adds nothing' and 'static image can only reference, cannot teach' framings were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; catalog fit rankings and product/tool-type labels were removed. No claim of one medium's superiority is intended.
The 'diamond' probe is retained as a counterexample: turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so a tilted square remains both a square and a rectangle.

The 'draw a square that is not a rectangle' probe is deliberately impossible; feedback now states this explicitly so the task is used to reveal the one-way asymmetry, not left as an answerable request.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a square and ask the child to PREDICT whether it will 'count as' a rectangle — and to say WHY before testing. Then together OBSERVE: check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler — four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel? It passes every test. Ask the child to EXPLAIN why the result differs from a prediction of 'no'. The stated reason before testing is the diagnostic part; a child who predicted 'no, it's too square' must now reconcile that with the square passing every rectangle test.
probeDeeper: 'You said a rectangle has four right angles and opposite sides equal — does it matter how long the sides are?' (pushes them to see length is not a defining property)
'Here is the square turned to look like a diamond — is it still a square? Is it still a rectangle?' (counterexample against orientation binding)
'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Now can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (the second is impossible — the asymmetry is the tell of real understanding)
'A square has four equal sides and four right angles — is it also a special rhombus? Why?' (transfer to the second inclusion)
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — a square is a rectangle. A rectangle needs four right angles and opposite sides that are equal and parallel; a square has all of those, plus its four sides happen to be equal too, so it is a special kind of rectangle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Exclusive/partition thinking: 'a square is not a rectangle — they're two different shapes' (each shape belongs in exactly one box)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a rectangle property checklist together and test the square against it item by item; use a nested Venn so the child sees the square can sit inside 'rectangle' without leaving 'square'. Reteach in place — this is the target concept.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a square and a rectangle are different kinds of shape
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, treats square and rectangle as separate named categories rather than comparing properties

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong prototype: 'a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides, so a square can't be one' (the unequal-sides look is wrongly treated as a defining property)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties (right angles, opposite sides equal/parallel) from typical appearance; show a range of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square so the prototype loosens. Revisit shape-property work.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the reason tier gives a definition of rectangle that requires it to be longer than it is wide

errorPatterns.pattern: One-box assumption: accepts that a square and a rectangle share properties yet still won't let one shape belong to two categories at once
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill the yes/no fact. Give more nested-set experience (Venn diagrams, 'all squares are inside the rectangle ring') and everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog and an animal at once) so the inclusion logic matures; it self-corrects with exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says something like 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' — a class-inclusion (part–whole) reasoning stage rather than a false fact

responseLevels.gap: Says a square is not a rectangle, or judges purely by appearance ('it's too square-looking'); cannot state the properties that define a rectangle.
responseLevels.full: Says yes and argues that the square passes every defining test of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and is therefore a special rectangle; extends the same reasoning to 'special rhombus', and can draw a quadrilateral that belongs to none of the subcategories.
responseLevels.partial: Says yes and can list shared features ('both have four sides / four corners') but does not use the defining properties to justify inclusion, and cannot transfer to 'square is a special rhombus' or explain why a rectangle need not be a square.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a square (and, alongside, an oblong rectangle). Ask: 'Is this square also a rectangle?' — then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes something a rectangle?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning from defining properties says yes and can name the rectangle tests the square passes. A child reasoning from appearance/prototype says no because the square doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle. The reason tier is decisive: a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'they both have four sides' is not mastery, and a confident 'no, a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide' exposes the prototype directly. Correct reasoning and prototype reasoning give genuinely different answers to 'what makes something a rectangle?'
